patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent right-sided weakness and dysphasia — second opinion after being told 'it's migraine'; parent recently had subarachnoid haemorrhage
patient.hpi:
A 36-year-old Black British man presented to the neurology clinic for a second opinion. He has had five episodes over the past 18 months of right-sided arm weakness, clumsiness and difficulty with word finding, lasting 20-35 minutes, each followed by a severe left-sided throbbing headache rated 9/10 with marked nausea and photophobia lasting 10-16 hours. The first episode was assessed at the emergency department and was diagnosed as 'likely TIA or hemiplegic migraine.' A normal CT head and a normal 24-hour Holter were performed. He was subsequently seen by a neurologist who diagnosed hemiplegic migraine and started propranolol 40 mg BID. Two further episodes occurred on propranolol.

New information from this visit: his father (aged 64) had a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) 8 weeks ago from a ruptured left MCA aneurysm. The patient is therefore seeking screening for intracranial aneurysm.

On re-review of his episodes: the motor and language deficit develops gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes, which he confirms on careful questioning. He has no family history of hemiplegic migraine. His sister has typical migraine without aura. He has mild hypertension (BP today 136/84). He is a non-smoker, occasional alcohol. He has no prior imaging of the intracranial vessels — only CT head was performed acutely.
pmh: No prior MRI or MRA performed

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

critical_actions: Brain MRI/MRA required (first hemiplegic migraine, family history of SAH)
Neurovascular referral for aneurysm risk-benefit (surveillance vs treatment)
Blood pressure optimisation (<130/80) — modifiable rupture risk factor
Avoid triptans and ergotamines in hemiplegic migraine and unruptured aneurysm
Counsel on warning signs of SAH (thunderclap headache, sudden severe deficit)
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe triptans or ergotamines
Do not anticoagulate without specific indication — increases rupture risk
Do not co-administer triptans with ergotamines
key_reasoning_points: Hemiplegic migraine requires MRI/MRA at first presentation — incidental aneurysm detection is a recognised consequence
Familial intracranial aneurysms (first-degree relative with SAH) carry higher rupture risk and warrant lower thresholds for treatment
Triptans are relatively contraindicated in both hemiplegic migraine and unruptured aneurysm

findings.description:
NEUROVASCULAR CONSULTATION — UNRUPTURED INTRACRANIAL ANEURYSM

Referral: 4 mm saccular aneurysm at left MCA bifurcation identified on MRA.

NEUROVASCULAR MDT ASSESSMENT:
  RUPTURE RISK: PHASES score for 4 mm MCA aneurysm in 36-year-old male, no prior SAH = PHASES score 4; estimated 5-year rupture risk approximately 3.0%.
  TREATMENT RISK: Surgical clipping or endovascular coiling at an experienced centre carries approximately 2-3% major morbidity/mortality for small MCA aneurysms of this size.
  ASSESSMENT: Treatment risk approximates natural history rupture risk at 5 years. Blood pressure is a modifiable risk factor for aneurysm growth and rupture. Imaging follow-up may be considered. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Familial Intracranial Aneurysm (FIA) — Screening Evidence

KEY FINDINGS:
1. DEFINITION: FIA is typically defined as ≥2 first- or second-degree relatives with intracranial aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage
2. SCREENING: UK and international guidelines recommend MRA screening for first-degree relatives of patients who have had SAH; relative risk is approximately 4x higher in first-degree relatives of affected individuals; further increased with ≥2 affected relatives
3. SCREENING AGE: First-degree relatives aged 20-70 are generally offered MRA screening; repeat intervals vary (commonly every 5-7 years if initially negative)
4. MODIFIABLE RISK FACTORS: Hypertension, smoking, and excessive alcohol intake are established modifiable risk factors for aneurysm growth and rupture in population studies

Clinical correlation recommended. First-degree relatives of SAH patients have approximately 4x increased intracranial aneurysm risk; screening with MRA is recommended; hypertension and smoking are key modifiable risk factors

LITERATURE SEARCH: Hemiplegic Migraine — Preventive Therapy Options

KEY FINDINGS:
1. PROPRANOLOL IN HEMIPLEGIC MIGRAINE: Beta-blockers have some supportive use in general migraine prevention; verapamil, topiramate, and acetazolamide have more specific evidence for hemiplegic migraine prevention
2. TRIPTAN USE IN HM: Triptans are cautioned (not absolutely contraindicated by all guidelines) in hemiplegic migraine due to vasoconstrictive mechanism during motor aura
3. PREVENTIVE OPTIONS AFTER PROPRANOLOL FAILURE: Topiramate (25-100 mg/day) and verapamil are commonly used second-line options in hemiplegic migraine
4. BLOOD PRESSURE: Hypertension is a well-established modifiable risk factor for both cardiovascular events and intracranial aneurysm rupture; adequate blood pressure management is important in this population

Clinical correlation recommended. Topiramate and verapamil are commonly used when propranolol is insufficient for hemiplegic migraine; triptans are cautioned; blood pressure management is important with comorbid vascular considerations

output.summary:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Blood Pressure Control and Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysm Risk

KEY FINDINGS:
1. HYPERTENSION AS RISK FACTOR: Hypertension is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for aneurysm growth and rupture (OR approximately 2.5-3.0 for SAH in hypertensive vs normotensive individuals in population studies)
2. BP TARGET: A target below 130/80 mmHg is generally recommended in guidelines for patients with known intracranial aneurysm
3. SMOKING: Tobacco smoking is independently associated with aneurysm formation and rupture risk
4. ALCOHOL: Heavy alcohol intake (more than 14 units/week) is associated with increased aneurysm rupture risk in population data

Clinical correlation recommended. Hypertension and smoking are the strongest modifiable risk factors for aneurysm rupture; blood pressure targets below 130/80 are generally recommended in patients with known intracranial aneurysm
